samples.text:
The diagram shows how a pumped-storage hydroelectric power station work. There are eight stages and they make a cycle, which happen every day and night.

At night, the demand for electricity is low, so the station takes the cheap surplus electricity from the grid. This electricity is used for pumping the water from the lower reservoir up to a tunnel. Then the water is stored in the upper reservoir on the top of the mountain.

During the day, the demand is high, so the valves are opened. After that the water is released and it flows down through the tunnel. Next, the falling water spin the turbines, which are connected to generators. Then the power is sent to the national grid.

Finally, the water is collected in the lower reservoir and it is ready to be pumped again at the next night. Overall, the station uses electricity at night and produces electricity in the day, and the same water is use again and again.
samples.why: Relevant overview but placed at the end · stages covered in order with basic day/night contrast · repetitive linking · adequate vocabulary · several agreement and preposition errors that do not obscure meaning.

samples.text:
The diagram illustrates the operation of a pumped-storage hydroelectric power station, which moves water between two reservoirs in order to meet changes in demand for electricity.

Overall, the process is cyclical and has eight stages. The key point is that the station uses electricity at night, when demand is low, and generates electricity during the day, when demand is high. In addition, the same water is used again and again.

At night, cheap surplus electricity is taken from grid and used to pump water from a lower reservoir up a tunnel to an upper reservoir, where it is stored at the top of a mountain. As a result, a large volume of water is kept high above the turbines, ready to be used later.

During the day, when there is greater demand for power, valves are opened and the water is released. It flows down through the tunnel, and the falling water spins turbines that are connected to generators. The electricity produced is then sent to the national grid. Finally, the water collects in the lower reservoir, where it remains until it is pumped back up again, and so the cycle repeat itself.
samples.why: Clear overview highlighting the night and day contrast · logical progression with varied cohesive devices · good collocations (surplus electricity, meet demand) · frequent error-free sentences with two minor slips.

samples.text:
The diagram explains how a pumped-storage hydroelectric plant functions over a cycle of night and day, using the same body of water repeatedly.

In essence, the system consists of eight repeating stages and operates in two distinct modes: during periods of low demand at night it consumes electricity to move water uphill, whereas during periods of high demand in the daytime it releases that water to generate power.

At night, inexpensive surplus electricity is drawn from the grid and used to pump water from the lower reservoir up through a tunnel. The water is then held in an upper reservoir on the mountain top, where it waits until it is needed. Crucially, this pumping phase relies on electricity at a time when it is both cheap and plentiful.

Once demand rises during the day, valves are opened and the water is allowed to flow back down the tunnel. As it falls, it drives turbines linked to generators, and the electricity this produces is fed into the national grid. The water then collects in the lower reservoir, where it remains until it can be pumped up once more, at which point the entire cycle resumes.
samples.why: Skilful overview contrasting the two operating modes · stages sequenced seamlessly with a clear return to the start · precise vocabulary (surplus, drawn from the grid) · wide range of complex structures · error-free.
